answer:
A WARNING is raised at **1,125 kW** of projected 15-minute demand.

**Why that level:** it is set at 90% of the 1,250 kW contract capacity [source: docs/knowledge/energy-management/EM-04_glossary.md#EM-04 Glossary > Billing and demand terms > Warning line]. This leaves a ~125 kW (10%) buffer so the shift supervisor can act to bring demand back under the contract before the 15-minute interval ends and an ALARM (above 1,250 kW) or a demand penalty would occur [source: docs/knowledge/energy-management/EM-02_demand_management.md#EM-02 Demand Management > Demand status tiers].

The WARNING tier also triggers if P(exceed next hour) ≥ 20%, even below 1,125 kW [source: docs/knowledge/energy-management/EM-02_demand_management.md#EM-02 Demand Management > Demand status tiers]. The 90% figure is chosen because summer normal peaks of 1,100–1,180 kW often put the plant close to this line on hot afternoons, so it serves as an early-warning margin rather than the hard limit.

answer:
Demand above the 1,250 kW contract is billed at a multiple of the period's contract price:

- Excess up to 10% over the contract (i.e., up to 1,375 kW) is billed at **contract price ×2**.
- Excess beyond that (above 1,375 kW) is billed at **contract price ×3**.

This is on top of the regular demand charge per kW of contract capacity (NT$223.60/kW/month in summer, NT$166.90/kW/month other months for the regular contract). [unverified citation removed]

The night-load baseline uses a CUSUM with **k = 0.5** (allowance) and **h = 8 robust sigmas** (alarm threshold), and it also requires the night load to be more than 3 kW above expectation before firing. [source: docs/knowledge/sop/SOP-04_compressed_air_leak.md#SOP-04 Compressed Air Leak > Trigger]

The load forecaster predicts the **change from an anchor** rather than the absolute demand level because of a limitation of tree models:

Tree models cannot predict a value above anything they saw in training, and the plant rarely exceeded its contract during the training period. A level-target model therefore tends to cap its predictions near historical norms and fails to warn about an exceedance — the first version with a level target actually missed the exceedances entirely. By predicting the *delta* on top of a known anchor (the last completed interval for short horizons 15 min–3 h, or the same time last week for day-ahead), the model can add a heat-driven or start-up-driven increment to the current load and flag a spike that exceeds anything in training. [source: docs/forecasting.md#Load forecasting > Model]

Two refinements keep the probability bands honest: sorting P10 ≤ P50 ≤ P90 per row to fix quantile crossing, and conformal widening — fitting on all but the last 14 days and scaling the band so 80% of those held-out days fall inside P10–P90. [source: docs/forecasting.md#Load forecasting > Model]

Weekday peak-period hours in summer (16 May – 15 October): **16:00–22:00**, at NT$9.39/kWh.

[source: docs/knowledge/energy-management/EM-03_tariff_guide.md#EM-03 Tariff Guide > Time-of-use periods and energy prices > Summer (16 May - 15 October)]

I now have the full picture. Here's the answer.

## On a hot afternoon with a forecast warning of exceeding the 1,250 kW contract

Follow **SOP-06 Heat Wave Pre-cooling**, which moves cooling energy earlier and avoids adding load in the peak window. The summer peak is 16:00–22:00 at NT$9.39/kWh; the half-peak (09:00–16:00) is NT$5.85/kWh.

**Before the peak (pre-cooling):**
- Run the chillers earlier / harder during the half-peak window to cool the building and chilled-water tank ahead of demand rising in the late afternoon.
- Confirm the EV-01 pause function works and warn staff at the EV bank that charging may be paused.
- Check compressor intake temperature and filters; fix known leaks first (SOP-04).

**At the peak (16:00–22:00):**
- Monitor projected demand every interval.
- **Pause EV charging as soon as WARNING is raised** — it removes up to 28 kW (100% of EV load) without touching production. Resume only when projected demand is back below 1,125 kW.
- If WARNING/ALARM is raised, follow **SOP-03** and shed in playbook order; raise the chilled-water setpoint by +1 °C (≈4% of chiller load) if the pre-cooling margin allows.
- Prepare to lower compressed-air pressure by 0.5 bar (≈3.5% of compressor load) if needed.

**Restore** shed actions in reverse order once demand is stable and below the 1,125 kW warning line — pressure, setpoint, burn-in loading, then EV charging; do not restore all at once.

Excess above contract is billed at 2× the period contract price up to 10% over, and 3× beyond.

**Note:** I can only read plant data and documents — I cannot operate equipment, change setpoints, or send operator messages. The above is the documented procedure for operators to carry out.

Here's the full picture:

**Peak demand:** 1,324.4 kW at 2025-06-16T08:15, which was 74 kW over the 1,250 kW contract [data: whatif_staggered_start]. Two consecutive 15-min intervals exceeded contract (1,307 kW at 08:00, 1,324 kW at 08:15) [data: list_detections].

**Cause:** A simultaneous start-up — 10 machines (805 kW rated) all started within a 3-minute window (07:57–08:27): both chiller compressors (CH-02), the large chiller, four injection moulders (IM-01 to IM-04), three reflow ovens (RF-01 to RF-03), the wave soldering machine (WS-01), and air compressor AC-02 [data: list_detections]. Their combined inrush stacked on top of the morning base load and pushed demand past contract.

**What 15-minute stagger would have achieved:** Re-simulation shows the peak would have dropped to 1,141.5 kW (a 182.9 kW reduction), keeping the plant under contract and avoiding the demand-exceedance penalty of up to NT$6,652 (US$208) [data: whatif_staggered_start].

Yes. A compressed-air leak was detected in September 2025.

**Detection:** Baseline layer, event AIR_LEAK on the compressor feeders AC-01, AC-02, AC-03. The leak began **2025-09-03** (night-load baseline), was flagged on **2025-09-09**, and ran continuously to 2025-10-01. Severity: medium.

**Size:** About **+18 kW** around the clock, up to 18.1 kW above the usual night base load. Estimated impact ~NT$652,462/year (US$20,389). [data: list_detections]

**Inspection procedure (SOP-04):**
1. **Detect** — the night-load baseline flags a rising compressor load; the loss shows most clearly at night when production demand is low.
2. **Tag** — tag each leak with a numbered tag; record location, type, and estimated size (small/medium/large); photograph where practical.
3. **Ultrasonic walk-down** — use an ultrasonic leak detector along main headers and branches; start where pneumatic use is heaviest (e.g. injection molding); check fittings, quick couplers, hoses, filter/regulator units, drain valves, blow-off nozzles, the air dryer area, and the compressor room.
4. **Tag** the leak with location, type, and size.
5. **Repair** — isolate and depressurize the section, replace the faulty fitting/hose/valve, re-pressurize and recheck with the detector, then remove the tag and record the closure.

Note: do not hide a leak by starting AC-02 — fix it. [source: docs/knowledge/sop/SOP-04_compressed_air_leak.md#SOP-04 Compressed Air Leak]

**Energy use (Fri 12:00 → Mon 12:00, 17–20 Oct 2025):** RF-02 used **1,976.9 kWh** (energy cost NT$6,045, energy charge only; demand charge and power-factor adjustment are separate). [data: get_energy]

**Weekend shutdown procedure for reflow ovens (SOP-02):**
- Reflow ovens must be switched **OFF, not left in standby** — a standby oven draws 36% of its 70 kW rating (≈25.2 kW) for as long as it stays on. A properly switched-off oven uses about 340–350 kWh per oven-weekend. [source: docs/knowledge/sop/SOP-02_weekend_shutdown.md#SOP-02 Weekend Shutdown > Why reflow ovens must be OFF, not standby]
- Keep ovens running 30 minutes after the line stops, then switch off — and only when no boards are inside. [source: docs/knowledge/sop/SOP-02_weekend_shutdown.md#SOP-02 Weekend Shutdown > Why reflow ovens must be OFF, not standby]
- After shutdown, verify each oven reads OFF (≤3% of rating) and that no reflow oven is IDLE or RUNNING; record plant base load (~500 kW; a much higher figure means something was left on). [source: docs/knowledge/sop/SOP-02_weekend_shutdown.md#SOP-02 Weekend Shutdown > Verification]

This matches the flag: RF-02 was left in standby all weekend (~1,556 kWh vs ~346 kWh normal, an excess of ~1,210 kWh), which is why it was over the 17–20 Oct window. [source: docs/knowledge/sop/SOP-02_weekend_shutdown.md#SOP-02 Weekend Shutdown > Why reflow ovens must be OFF, not standby]

Here's what happened.

**What happened:** MDB-3's power factor collapsed on 5 November as part of incident S8, the capacitor-bank fault that ran 3–13 November. Before S8 the board ran near 0.96; during S8 it fell to about 0.84–0.85 all day.

**Daytime PF on 5 November (08:00–17:00):** mean 0.849, range 0.845–0.852, flat across the shift [data: get_meter_series]. That matches the "capacitor bank out of service" level in SOP-05, well below the 0.90 rule threshold and approaching the 0.80 surcharge line [source: docs/knowledge/sop/SOP-05_power_factor_check.md#SOP-05 Power Factor Check > Expected PF values].

**Maintenance should check (per SOP-05):** the capacitor bank on MDB-3 for an out-of-service condition — specifically a tripped breaker or a blown fuse — and restore it to service. Healthy MDB-3 with the bank in service is ~0.96 [source: docs/knowledge/sop/SOP-05_power_factor_check.md#SOP-05 Power Factor Check > Purpose].
